bib.title: Deep Bayesian Bandits Showdown: An Empirical Comparison of Bayesian Deep Networks for Thompson Sampling

read.skipped: Tables 4-8 and 10 (per-algorithm numeric cells) were read only in part (headers, first rows, selected rows); Table 1/6/9 read for the rows cited.

question: How does the quality of an approximate posterior (from different Bayesian deep-network methods) affect Thompson Sampling performance in contextual bandits?
hypothesis: Implied: good posterior approximations should give good Thompson Sampling decisions, but partially optimised/slowly converging uncertainty estimates may hurt in the online setting.
contributions: A benchmark of approximate-posterior methods under Thompson Sampling on contextual bandits (real-data and synthetic wheel bandit).
Finding that methods that couple representation and uncertainty (VI, BB alpha-divergence, SGLD-type MCMC) suffer from partial optimisation online.
Finding that Bayesian linear regression on the last-layer representation (NeuralLinear) is robust and easy to tune.

method.summary: Eight real-data contextual bandits plus a synthetic Wheel bandit are used to compare about 15 posterior-approximation families (linear, NeuralLinear, RMS greedy, BBB, black-box alpha-divergence, dropout, SGFS, constant SGD, bootstrap, parameter noise, GP), each in a default and two Bayesian-optimised hyperparameter versions. All neural methods share one 2x100 ReLU MLP. Cumulative and simple regret are reported relative to a Uniform policy over 50 shuffled runs.

datasets.name: Mushroom
datasets.source: Schlimmer 1981; 22 attributes, two classes; reward +5 safe, +5 w.p. 1/2 else -35 poisonous, 0 if not eaten

datasets.name: Statlog (Shuttle)
datasets.source: UCI (Asuncion & Newman 2007); reward 1 if correct; one action optimal ~80% of cases

datasets.name: Financial
datasets.source: authors' own: stock prices of 21 NYSE/Nasdaq companies, 14 years; arms are synthetic linear combinations (portfolios)
datasets.preprocessing: context = price difference between start and end of session per stock

datasets.name: Jester
datasets.source: Goldberg et al. 2001; complete subset of users rating all 40 jokes
datasets.preprocessing: d = 32 ratings as context, k = 8 as arms (following Riquelme et al. 2017)

datasets.name: Song (YearPredictionMSD)
datasets.preprocessing: years 1922-2011 split into 10 equal-count buckets; decreasing Gaussian reward by bucket distance

datasets.name: Wheel bandit (synthetic)
datasets.source: d = 2, k = 5, delta from 0.5 to 0.99 (Tables 9, 10); contexts uniform in unit circle; mu1 = 1.2, mu2 = 1.0, mu3 = 50.0, sigma = 0.01

models.name: Shared MLP (RMS/NeuralLinear/BBB/dropout/bootstrap/etc.)
models.architecture: fully connected, 2 hidden layers of 100 units, ReLU; input dim d, k outputs

models.name: NeuralLinear
models.architecture: RMS2 network; exact Bayesian linear regression (inverse-gamma noise, Gaussian beta) per action on last-hidden-layer output; regression updated every step, network every tf steps, forward pass over all data after retrain

models.name: Linear posterior family (LinPost, LinFullPost, Diag, PrecisionDiag variants)
models.architecture: closed-form Bayesian linear regression per action

models.name: GP
models.architecture: multi-task GP, Matern 3/2 x linear x task kernel; inputs stop after 1000 observations; sparse variational GP with 300 inducing points tried but not reported

training.objective: Per method: MSE-style regression on observed action for RMS-based nets; ELBO for BBB; black-box alpha-divergence; SGLD-type updates (SGFS, constant SGD); only loss of the observed action is used
training.optimizer: RMSProp for RMS-based networks (RMS1 lr 0.01 fixed; RMS2 decaying, reset each period; RMS3 decaying, not reset, starts at 1); SGFS/constSGD use their own updates
training.lr: method-specific, see Table 2 (e.g. RMS initial lr 1.0, decay 0.55)
training.lr_schedule: RMS2/RMS3 decay; BBB and alpha-divergence ts linearly decayed from 10000 over first 100 times
training.warmup: each action pulled s = 3 times round-robin initially
training.steps: default ts = 20 or 100 mini-batches every tf = 20 timesteps
training.regularisation: no data buffer (catastrophic forgetting observed); all observations sampled uniformly into mini-batches
training.compute: relative elapsed time only (Table 8, normalised to RMS = 100)

other.hyperparameter_versions: default guess, plus -MR (Bayesian optimisation on Mushroom) and -SL (on Statlog)

inference.decoding: Thompson Sampling: sample model from approximate posterior, act greedily
inference.samples: 50 independent runs with reshuffled context order

parameters.bootstrap: q in {5,10}, p in {0.8,1.0} mainly tested; final q=10,p=1.0 (default), q=2,p=0.95 (MR), q=3,p=0.92 (SL)

metrics.name: Cumulative regret
metrics.definition: E[r* - r], r* = reward of optimal policy over n rounds; reported normalised to Uniform = 100

metrics.name: Simple regret
metrics.definition: mean cumulative regret over the last 500 time-steps, proxy for final policy quality

metrics.name: Mean rank
metrics.definition: rank across the suite of bandit problems

eval.protocol: 50 trials with context order reshuffled; mean and standard error of the mean; rewards deterministic for most real datasets so regret uses best realised reward.

availability.data: public UCI/Jester/Million Song datasets; Financial dataset is authors' own

evidence.quote: The size of each mini-batch was 512.

results.claim: On the Wheel bandit at delta=0.99, NeuralLinear has cumulative regret about half of Uniform's while RMS and its spinoffs are near or above Uniform.
results.setup: Wheel bandit, delta = 0.99, cumulative regret normalised to Uniform=100, mean over 50 trials
results.note: SGFS is lower at 45.55 in the same column; NeuralLinear-MR 49.63.

results.claim: SGFS has the lowest listed cumulative regret in the delta=0.99 Wheel column among the rows read, below NeuralLinear.
On easy Wheel setting delta=0.5 NeuralLinear is near-optimal.
NeuralLinear nearly solves Statlog, which needs non-linearity, where linear approaches fail.
results.setup: Statlog bandit, n=43500, cumulative regret normalised to Uniform

results.claim: NeuralLinear on Mushroom beats the RMS network it is built on.
On Jester NeuralLinear is no better than RMS (worse).
By mean rank over the datasets, NeuralLinear (22) is behind the exact linear methods (LinFullPost 13.9, LinFullDiagPrecPost 14.3).
results.table: Table 1, row LinFullPost, column Mean Rank
results.note: Mean rank is over the whole suite per Fig 5 and Table 1; lower is better.

results.claim: Tuned parameter noise improves average rank over the RMS learner it is based on.
Hyperparameter search for BootstrappedNN chose only 2 and 3 networks, versus 10 in the manual version, without losing performance.
results.quote: decided to use only q = 2 and q = 3 networks respectively

results.claim: For BBB on a linear model, more training epochs per step slowly improve regret but never match the exact mean-field solution (PrecisionDiag).
results.setup: Fig 4: linear data d=10, k=6, and Statlog; BBB with epochs 20-1000, fixed noise sigma=0.75
results.quote: As the number of training epochs increases, BBB improves performance, but is always outperformed by PrecisionDiag.

results.claim: Diagonalising the precision matrix (mean-field) performs dramatically better than diagonalising the covariance in linear Thompson Sampling.
results.setup: linear bandits k=20, d=15 and 30, real data

results.claim: NeuralLinear is fast computationally relative to others.
results.note: Roughly 1.4 to 2.4 times RMS across datasets; text calls it fast.

results.claim: Wheel bandit problem is set up so that exploration need grows with delta.
Overall conclusion: slowly converging uncertainty estimates are a problem online; decoupling representation from uncertainty helps.

limits: Authors concede they did not add a baseline with dropout only during training, so exploration vs training benefit is not disentangled.
Hyperparameters tuned on Mushroom or Statlog (MR/SL) so these versions are not independent of the eval sets.
Only contextual bandits, not full RL; authors suggest trying NeuralLinear in complex RL domains.
GP limited to first 1000 observations; sparse GP not reported.
Mean rank favours exact linear methods over NeuralLinear on several datasets; the NeuralLinear-best claim is qualitative and strongest on Wheel (where SGFS is lower at delta 0.99).
Weak claim of reason for NeuralLinear success ('We suspect') is untested.
Code was promised 'will be available'; no hardware or compute stated.
Datasets are small (Financial n=3713) and Thompson Sampling ignores horizon.

terms.definition: Bayesian linear regression on the last-hidden-layer representation of a neural network, used for Thompson Sampling; network and regression updated at different time-scales.
approximated as the mean cumulative regret in the last 500 time-steps
